USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Use the Osaka window to restart substantive talks without new commitments and without firing List 4. Keep the existing 25% tariffs on ~$250B and the Huawei Entity List as leverage; license only non-sensitive sales. Press Beijing to convert the farm-purchase talk into actual orders and to put IP, forced tech transfer, subsidies, and a real enforcement mechanism back on the table. Do not roll back tariffs or trade Huawei relief for atmospherics while those structural issues remain open.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: Threat is real but not economy-wide. China walked back a near-finished text in early May, prompting the List 3 hike to 25% on 10 May and the Huawei Entity List on 16 May; those moves, plus China's matching tariff hike on ~$60B of US goods, rare-earth signaling, and an announced unreliable-entity list, leave IP theft, forced tech transfer, and industrial-policy practices unremedied (timeline 2019-05-05 through 2019-05-31). US agriculture is the exposed sector: farm exports to China have collapsed (on the order of $26B to ~$6B), soybean trade was driven toward zero, and USDA had to announce a second, $16B aid package on 23 May because retaliation hit soy, pork, and other farm-belt products. That is material political and sectoral damage, not a full GDP crisis: Michigan sentiment is still 98.4, VIX has fallen back to ~14 after the mid-May spike, and CPI is contained. The warning lights are financial and industrial, not consumer: 10-year yields are down ~68bp to 2.06%, the 2-year is at 1.83%, industrial production has slipped ~0.9% over the window, and the goods deficit remains ~$73B with July China imports still ~$41B versus ~$8.7B of US exports. Osaka (29 Jun) only paused List 4 (~$300B of consumer goods already through June hearings) and left Huawei on the Entity List; by 9 Jul, Lighthizer/Mnuchin/Liu He had only a constructive scheduling call, farm purchases had not materialized beyond a token rice order, and Commerce was still treating Huawei as blacklisted. Escalating now would break a two-week-old pause, hit US households (phones, apparel, toys) and invite rare-earth or further ag retaliation. Conceding now would reward the May walk-back. Negotiate from the current posture.
key_factors: May collapse of near-deal text and List 3 hike to 25% left structural IP/tech-transfer/enforcement issues unresolved
Huawei Entity List plus China's rare-earth signal and unreliable-entity list keep a national-security/tech channel open alongside tariffs
US farm-belt is the retaliatory pressure point ($16B USDA aid; soybean/export collapse) while the consumer economy is still intact
Osaka pause parked List 4 and talks just restarted with no firm Chinese purchase or legal-change commitments
Softening industrial production and a much flatter Treasury curve raise the cost of a consumer-facing List 4 escalation

Talks relaunch with little changed since the May breakdown; Chinese side did not make firm immediate farm-purchase commitments; Huawei still treated as blacklisted pending licenses.

CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Resume substantive talks on the Osaka track without new tariff or entity-list strikes and without unilateral purchase or legal concessions. Keep existing retaliatory tariffs in place as leverage, hold the unreliable-entity list and rare-earth threats in reserve, and press for concrete Huawei licensing plus a path off the remaining ~$300B tariff threat. The aim is to keep List 4 off the table and test whether Washington will trade limited Huawei relief and a tariff freeze for purchase discussions, not to reopen the May draft on sovereignty-sensitive legal changes.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: Threat is high, not existential. After the May 10 hike of List 3 to 25%, combined U.S. Section 301 coverage is ~$250B of Chinese exports, and the May 16 Entity List plus Google/chip cutoffs hit Huawei—the core of China’s 5G and tech-autonomy agenda (timeline 2019-05-10, 2019-05-16, 2019-05-20). Q2 GDP slowed to 6.2%, a 27-year low, H1 exports to the U.S. fell 8.1%, and June factories were shedding jobs at the fastest pace since the GFC, while CNY weakened from ~6.73 in early May to a mid-May peak near 6.92 after the hike (CNBC/Reuters 2019-07-15; DEXCHUS). That maps to the CHN +0.5 anchor (export sectors hit, FX pressure, firm-level Huawei targeting, export-hub employment risk). It is not +1.0: reserves remain ~$3.12T, the discount rate is unchanged at 2.9%, CPI is stable, official H1 growth is still inside the 6.0–6.5% band, June IP rebounded to 6.3%, and Osaka paused the threatened ~$300B consumer-goods list (country_health TRESEG/INTDSR/CHNPRINTO; timeline 2019-06-29). Action should stay near zero because another Chinese escalation (UEL implementation, rare-earth cutoff, broader tariffs) would likely invite the List 4 hike Trump already prepared and would lock Huawei into a presumption-of-denial regime just as Commerce is only beginning to talk licenses (Ross 2019-07-09/10; Reuters staff still treating Huawei as blacklisted). Unilateral concede_purchases is also wrong: Chinese sources said Xi did not lock in immediate farm buys, and Beijing has tied any purchases to tariff removal; giving them now would replay the May collapse without getting List 3 off 25%. The July 9 Lighthizer–Mnuchin–Liu He call was only “constructive,” with Kudlow warning there are “no miracles” and a large gap still on the May legal-text/enforcement issues. Negotiate—talks without new commitments—is the stance that uses the truce, probes Huawei license scope before the Aug. 19 TGL expiry, and avoids either looking weak at home or handing Washington a pretext to tariff the rest of the export book.
key_factors: List 3 now at 25% on ~$200B; combined U.S. tariffs cover ~$250B of Chinese goods
Huawei and affiliates remain on the Entity List; Osaka relief is licenses under presumption of denial, not delisting
Q2 GDP 6.2% (27-year low), H1 exports to U.S. -8.1%, June factory job cuts; FX pressure peaked in May then stabilized
Osaka pause on the threatened ~$300B List 4 and July 9 phone talks reopen a negotiation channel
China’s buffers (reserves ~$3.12T, CPI stable, growth still inside 6.0–6.5%) make further escalation unnecessary and risky
Structural/sovereignty gap from the May draft remains; no matching U.S. tariff offer that would justify purchase concessions
